meta.titre: Specific heat capacity: Q = mc(delta theta), heaters and mixtures

sections.contenu_markdown: At the seaside in Limbe, the sand is burning hot at midday, yet the sea water a few steps away stays pleasantly cool. A mechanic in Bamenda pours water into a car radiator because it carries a lot of heat away without becoming dangerously hot. Different materials need different amounts of heat to warm up by the same number of degrees. That property is the specific heat capacity, and the GCE O/L asks for its definition, for calculations with $Q = mc\Delta\theta$ and for the electrical experiment to measure it.

items: Energy is measured in joules (J), and power is the rate of energy transfer: $P = E/t$, in watts (W).
Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius ($^\circ\mathrm{C}$); a temperature change of $1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ equals a change of $1\ \mathrm{K}$.
Mass must be converted into kilograms: $1000\ \mathrm{g} = 1\ \mathrm{kg}$.

sections.titre: Specific heat capacity and heat calculations
sections.contenu_markdown:
The **specific heat capacity** $c$ of a substance is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the substance by $1\ \mathrm{K}$ (or $1\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Its unit is $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

$$Q = mc\Delta\theta$$

- $Q$ is the heat gained or lost in joules, $m$ the mass in kg and $\Delta\theta$ the temperature change (final minus initial).
- For water, $c = 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$: it takes $4200\ \mathrm{J}$ to warm $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water by $1\ \mathrm{K}$.
- When the heat comes from an electric heater of power $P$ working for a time $t$ (in seconds), assuming no heat is lost: $Q = Pt = VIt$.

The **heat capacity** $C$ of a body is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the *whole body* by $1\ \mathrm{K}$: $C = mc$, in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Specific heat capacity refers to $1\ \mathrm{kg}$; heat capacity refers to the whole object.

Water has a high specific heat capacity. It can absorb a large amount of heat for a small rise in temperature, so it is a good coolant in car radiators and a good heat store in hot-water systems. It also keeps coastal regions cooler by day than inland areas, since it warms up slowly.

**Mixing.** If no heat is lost to the surroundings, heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body:

$$m_1 c_1 (\theta_1 - \theta_f) = m_2 c_2 (\theta_f - \theta_2)$$

variantes.nom: Electrical method for a solid block
variantes.quand_utiliser: When you are asked to describe an experiment to find the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Apparatus: metal block with two holes, immersion heater, thermometer, joulemeter or ammeter, voltmeter and stopwatch, balance, lagging, a few drops of oil. Weigh the block to find $m$. Put the heater and thermometer in the holes (a drop of oil improves contact) and wrap the block in lagging. Record the initial temperature, switch on the heater for a time $t$ while reading $V$ and $I$, then record the highest temperature. Then $c = \dfrac{VIt}{m\Delta\theta}$. Precautions: lag the block to reduce heat loss, wait for the highest temperature before reading it, and use the same thermometer for both readings.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a hot solid is dropped into cold water, or two liquids at different temperatures are mixed.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write 'heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body', and use the final temperature $\theta_f$ for both bodies. If the container also absorbs heat, include it, otherwise the value found for the hot body is too small.

sections.enonce_markdown: An electric heater of power $800\ \mathrm{W}$ is used to raise the temperature of an aluminium block of mass $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ from $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is $900\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the heat gained by the block. (b) Find the time for which the heater must be on if no heat is lost. (c) Find the time if only $90\%$ of the electrical energy reaches the block. (d) Find the heat capacity of the block.

etapes.action: Find the time with no heat loss.

etapes.justification: Only $0.90 P t$ reaches the block, so $0.90 P t = Q$.

etapes.action: Find the heat capacity of the block.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The block gains **54 000 J**; the heater takes **67.5 s** with no loss and **75 s** if 90 % of its energy reaches the block; the heat capacity of the block is **1 350 J/K**.

items.erreur_markdown: A student uses a mass of 500 g directly in $Q = mc\Delta\theta$ with $c = 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The unit of $c$ contains kilograms, so the mass must be in kg. Using 500 instead of 0.5 gives an answer 1000 times too large.

items.erreur_markdown: A student calculates the heat to warm water from $24\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $64\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using $\Delta\theta = 64$.
items.pourquoi_faux: $\Delta\theta$ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature.

items.erreur_markdown: A heater of power 2.0 kW is on for 4 minutes and the student writes $Q = 2000 \times 4 = 8000\ \mathrm{J}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The time must be in seconds when power is in watts.

items.erreur_markdown: A student defines specific heat capacity as the heat needed to raise the temperature of a substance by one degree.
items.pourquoi_faux: The definition is incomplete: it must state the unit mass (1 kg). Without that it is the heat capacity of the whole object.
items.correction_markdown: Define it as the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 K.

items.enonce_markdown: Calculate the heat needed to raise the temperature of $2.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water from $24\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $64\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Use $c = 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for water.

An immersion heater rated $2.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ is used to heat $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water from $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming that all the heat goes into the water, calculate the heat required and the time taken. Give the time in minutes and seconds.
items.solution_markdown:
$Q = mc\Delta\theta = 3.0 \times 4200 \times (60 - 20) = 504\,000\ \mathrm{J}$.

The power is $2.0\ \mathrm{kW} = 2000\ \mathrm{W}$ and $Q = Pt$, so $t = \dfrac{Q}{P} = \dfrac{504\,000}{2000} = 252\ \mathrm{s}$.

$252 = 4 \times 60 + 12$, that is 4 minutes 12 seconds.

**Heat required = 504 000 J; time = 252 s = 4 min 12 s.**

items.enonce_markdown: A metal block of mass $0.20\ \mathrm{kg}$ is heated to $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and dropped into $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in a well-lagged container of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature is $25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (a) Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal. (b) If the container had absorbed some heat, would the true value of the specific heat capacity be greater or less than your answer? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Heat gained by water $= 0.50 \times 4200 \times (25 - 20) = 10\,500\ \mathrm{J}$.

Heat lost by metal $= 0.20 \times c \times (100 - 25) = 0.20 \times c \times 75 = 15c$.

Heat lost $=$ heat gained: $15c = 10\,500$, so $c = \dfrac{10\,500}{15} = 700\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

**c = 700 J/kg/K.**

(b) If the container also absorbed heat, the metal would have lost more than the water gained. So the heat lost by the metal is greater than $10\,500\ \mathrm{J}$, and the true $c$ is **greater** than $700\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

items_markdown: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of a substance by $1\ \mathrm{K}$; $Q = mc\Delta\theta$; water: $4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
Heat capacity $C = mc$ (in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$) refers to the whole body; specific heat capacity refers to $1\ \mathrm{kg}$.
Electrical heating: $Q = Pt = VIt$ with time in seconds; if heat is lost, only part of $Pt$ reaches the body.
In mixtures, heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body, at the same final temperature.
Water's high specific heat capacity makes it a good coolant (car radiators) and heat store, and it moderates coastal climates.
